author: @biocalicoe
text:
I wouldn't go so easily with the BYD. 
I mean, I love the looks, interior and ergonomics of the BYD rather than the Tesla.
But I have watched other tests, some of them driven by actual engineers and test drivers and the BYD, even the AWD, is much focused on comfort rather than road handling.
Also, the software in the Tesla is years ahead of the BYD. Some people say that this can be fixed, however the BYD is using regular Android, which I think will limit its capability to be updated in the future (note, this is not Android Automotive, whoever who has owned an Honda will know what and Android system works).
Nevertheless, ADAS are much worse than a Tesla or any other major brand. Have you tried to disable the speed alarm? In the Tesla is just one touch, in the BYD you have to dive into 3 menus. And you have to do this every time you start the car.
The battery is bigger but the car is less efficient and the range is aligned with a Model 3 SR (and much lower than a LR).
And I have questions about how the APP works. This is something crucial in EVs to control charge and pre-climate and the Tesla APP works smoothly.
On the other hand, the BYD has a radar, camera, a proper rain sensor and parking sensors. Not so cool as the Tesla Vision but should work better is everything is calibrated properly.

I mean, I love and hate both cars. Both have good arguments to buy and to discard them. Just disagreeing in a so categoric answer.
Maybe if Tesla creates a sub-brand with "normal" designs and ergonomics...

text:
I first watched this video with increasing amazement and later, to make sure I had seen and heard all of this correctly, again. And which by the way will never or can never be completely perfect in all respects because: humans at work.

It is more honest to make an inventory of the different properties and compare them with each other. That comes across as more sincere in terms of content than a story full of vitriol, full of pretended benevolence, excellently written, that's for sure, but here and there ostentatiously over-acted. I have a Model Y but the seats in the Seal do look more comfortable but my seats are way more comfortable than my gas car so I love them.

The lack of stalks on the Tesla was a bad idea this brings the BYD back into play - overall as cars I think they are pretty close - (personal styling preferences aside I think the new Tesla is massively better looking than the BYD which I think already looks really dated)

The thing that swings the equation big time back in Tesal's favour is tech & charging - with the latest update the Tesla will gather all of the data for all other Tesla's following similar routes to your journey and using AI will detrmine the best charger & charging strategy to get you to your destination in the shortest possible time by aggregating all of the information it has on who is likely to reach chargers at what time and for how long they will spend there. BYD are nowhere near this level of sophistication - but in Australia they are also $3k cheaper like for like and they also have a $10k cheaper base model - tough choice but I would go with the Tesla (and even more so if it had stalks)

text:
Nice to have a review on the RWD Seal, as most reviews are on the AWD version, but finally a few are coming through on the RWD version.

作为一个中国的海豹车主我表达一下我的看法（我就懒得写英语了，反正你们可以用谷歌翻译），特斯拉在上海的销量非常的好，所以我可以很容易的从我的朋友那试驾他们的model3和model Y ，通过试驾我自己体会了记得让我很不舒服的地方，1. 特斯拉没有专门的仪表盘，这让我不得不在行驶过程中不停的看中央屏幕来获取速度信息避免超速。 2. 单踏板模式，我非常不理解单踏板给你们（欧洲人/美州人）带来的所谓便利性，在我看来这会让一个习惯了传统汽车驾驶的司机在使用特斯拉时变成一个马路杀手（中国的汽车驾驶培训告诉我们的驾驶方式是非常根深蒂固的）。3. 特斯拉的内饰， （尽管我还没有尝试过新的model3听说他升级了不错的内饰）特斯拉对于内饰的偷工减料简直是在犯罪 他们用20多万RMB的价格卖出的汽车  内饰甚至不如一台10万RMB的大众汽车。
回到我选择比亚迪的理由 1. 作为一个中国汽车品牌，他在中国的售价确实比较的划算。 2.  比亚迪的充电协议使它支持中国市场上可以看到的所有充电桩（包括特斯拉的特高压800V超级充电桩，顺便说一句中国的公共充电桩数量超过全世界的总和）3. 海豹的驾驶感受更像一台汽油动力的轿车。4. 很多评论中提到的能量回收的可调节范围 海豹有高动能回收和普通回收两个档位，你们可以从屏幕左下角的汽车小标识点击进入后设置。 5.  虽然比亚迪的智能化水平在中国电动车厂家里算是一个悲剧但是他的语音识别能力还是不错的，很多时候你们可以直接通过语音发布指令。

text: As someone in Australia comparing the same models, what tipped the balance for you if you don’t mind saying?

author: @LukeyLuke77
text:
@newbris I test drove the Model 3 RWD and LR for 45mins each. There’s absolutely no doubts there’s a huge upgrade over the previous Model 3 and does everything better.

The main talking point is obviously the stalk removal. Gave them a good workout in varying scenarios and while they weren’t really an issue and it took minimal time to get use to them there were times where they were simply an inconvenience and these situations can’t be avoided based simply on hand/wheel positioning.

Ride comfort and cabin noise improvements are certainly noticeable on smooth roads but still got some noise at highway speeds.

The main issue but not really an issue given it’s in beta was the auto-gear selector. Only got to try it a few times but on a couple of occasions it made the wrong selection and if you were none-the-wiser it could be a rather ominous outcome. I have seen previous videos where Tesla Vision has grossly misjudged objects and measurements so hopefully there’s improvements there.

The other things I’m not a big fan of: gear selection on the centre screen, exterior looks, everything on the centre screen and completely minimalist look and feel.

Overall I was impressed with the upgraded Model 3 but ultimately, I still prefer the look of both the interior and exterior of the Seal and for the money, I still can’t go past it. The (Tesla) RWD in my preferred config would be $70K ($64K after the rebate) and the LR would be $80K while the Seal Performance is $72K.

text:
What a great review. None of the BS about 0-60 times and drag races. Just a lot of practical comparisons on things that would affect everyday driving.
I have just had the chance to sit in the Seal and inspect the interior and have a play around with the infotainment and controls. As a current Tesla Model 3 owner I was quite impressed. I just know intuitively where the controls are. By the same token, the scroll wheels on the Model 3 steering wheel fall easily under your thumb and don’t require you to look for them like the buttons on the ‘conventional’ steering wheel of the Seal. I struggled with the lack of driver’s display in the Tesla so much, I have fitted an aftermarket HUD.
Seriously considering changing my Model 3 for a Seal next year. While the Supercharger network is good, 95% of my charging is at home.

Great review.  Thank you!

You mention that too much functionality is through the screens on both cars, and I agree.  

I haven't driven either of these cars, but I've driven a lot of previous model Model 3s and a lot of BYD Atto 3s.  

On those cars, I found that the lack of buttons was far more of a problem in the Tesla than in the BYD, even if you don't allow for the BYD having more non-screen controls.  The BYD's voice recognition was excellent, so you could say, "turn off air conditioning, set fan speed to 2, and set temperature to 18 degrees" for example, and it would do it.

I'd still prefer buttons.  But the BYD offers a more usable alternative to the screen than the Tesla does.

text: The reason why BYD doesn't offer 1-Pedal driving is because the majority of the drivers simply don't like this feature. It feels unnatural to most people. I am sure after getting used to it, more people might be OK with this feature. BYD did actually incorporate the regenerative braking benefit of "1-Pedal Driving" into the braking system itself. In the BYD Seal, the regen kicks in when you first step on the brake pedal. The actual friction braking will eventually take over if the braking force required exceeds the regen capability. BYD's system works flawlessly. The ultimate goal is to recuperate as much kinetic energy as possible, and the regenerative braking system in the BYD Seal achieves this efficiently. All drivers are used to "coasting" as a natural part of driving. BYD wanted to preserve this feeling, and I am so glad they did that. One of BYD's major goal has always been to make the transition from ICE cars to EVs as seamless as possible. That's why they outsell all their competitors in China by a huge margin (including Tesla).

text: 53k miles on a M3, extended test drive on the BYD Seal. The BYD is definitely a more comfortable car to travel in with great quality materials and ride comfort and sound insulation. I also think the BYD looks a bit better. The cabin and the seats are top quality and the exterior is also really nice, looks even better in person. But the M3 (even the old one) is just a bit more fun to drive. Its direct and darty (which I like) charges WAY faster, has the network and also a very large service network. The BYD is in its infancy, driving 100 miles to a service centre at the moment isnt ideal....UI wise the Teslas are also miles ahead. Menus make sense and are intuitive and grouped properly ie Climate/Display/Controls etc. The BYD has a bit of everything everywhere. Menus, pull downs, side swipes. That being said the Seals central screen is something special its so large and so crisp when navigating its a joy. Its also worth noting according BYD any Seals shipped before March come with the indicator on the right stalk and wipers on the left. My test car had this and was a nightmare to adjust to. Apparently the norm in other right drive markets. It also has the most aggressive lane departure system Ive ever seen (Even more aggressive than the MG4). Even an few inches left or right of centre it was dragging you all over the place. Can be turned off no doubt but needs adjusting. Id deffo still recommend it but I think it still needs some maturity and bug ironing to make it a sure thing. Most of that can be done through software so should be easy. Credit to them though honestly it rides as well a C Class/3 Series maybe even a smidgeon better. There arent many EVs that can do that. The new Tesla indicator is a no go for me too 🤣 the New M3 ups its quality considerably but not enough to tempt me for one either... so I'll be hanging on to my old M3 for now. If anyone has one, that would be my advice, especially if like me you still have ultrasonic sensors 🤣 (If you know you know....)

author: @sjwright2
text:
You can still play music from a USB on a newer Model 3, but it requires some trickery. If you're comfortable with computers, you could replace the sentry USB stick in the glovebox with a larger device, ideally a "real" SSD (which use higher quality flash memory that's far more durable than any USB stick). Connect it to a computer and format it with two partitions, one for sentry and another for music.

Or you can connect a hub in the glovebox USB port, use one port for the sentry USB stick and another for your music. Tesla explicitly advises against this, however.

Finally there are aftermarket USB port modules for the centre console which give you more ports including one which supports data connections.

author: @EVinstructor
text:
When Tesla announced the new Model 3 with switches for indicators as a driver trainer I started to think about the implications for driving safely. You can be sure if Tesla is doing this other manufacturers will follow. It keeps production costs down and some legacy manufacturers need to find savings if they stand any chance of avoiding bankruptcy in the transition to EVs. 

So I started to watch my trainees with indicator buttons in mind. After a couple of Nissan Leafs I now own a Model 3. Surprisingly I noticed there’s a lot of times when trainees have to let go of the steering wheel with their left hand and move it back to the stalk when their hand would be next to the buttons if they kept hold of the wheel. I’ll qualify this with the fact that a Model 3 only does one turn to lock and is very responsive. Rarely was anyone more than a quarter turn from straight when they needed to indicate. The right turn on a roundabout and signalling left to leave is the example that could cause problems because I noticed the steering wheel was generally upside down at this point.

So I thought about this right turn on a roundabout and the upside down steering wheel. Then I noticed myself subconsciously turning the radio volume up on the steering wheel control whatever way it’s pointing. Upside down, sideways, it doesn’t matter where the steering is pointing I’ve developed the skill of using that control. My conclusion is button indicators are just a different skill. A new learner who only ever saw that system would probably find stalks weird. I equate it to training I’ve done with experienced licence holders of many years first encountering an automatic. They are perplexed initially but like it when they get used to it. 

The Tesla Model 3 does divide opinion. Personally, I love it. I find the minimalist interior calming and a very nice place to spend the day. The lack of clutter in the car focuses trainees minds. When it’s not doing it’s day job I really like the firm ride and direct steering. I also think it’s a good looking car. The Supercharger network is a number 1 reason to get a Tesla, drive anywhere with no concern about charging. 

However, people have different tastes and we need a cars to cater for different tastes. Legacy manufacturers can’t get near Tesla despite trying hard. The worlds top selling car this year will be the Model Y and Tesla will sell almost as many cars as BMW or Mercedes, that’s cars regardless of powertrains not just EVs. We need a new competitive car market to emerge. BYD look like they will be commercial challengers to Tesla. The Seal is a good competitor, similar but different appealing to different customers. Those that feel reassured by a car closer to the ICE they’re giving up on will feel more comfortable with the Seal.  BYD will also be filling the low end sector with the Seagull and Dolphin where Tesla have no models as yet. The thing about this is that the new world car market will be dominated by the Chinese and Tesla. Interesting times.

At least as far as the boot goes, as a family it would definitely be easier for us with a M3 but if I truly cared that much I also wouldn't be buying a sedan but an SUV. The interior space storage wise is a lot more usable on the Seal on the other hand, with more nooks and crannies to store stuff. 

- In terms of charging faster, the difference in peak charge rate is only 20kw which is much of muchness. Yes the M3 charges faster but that has more to do with the size of the batteries, with the Seal Premium having a 20kw bigger battery. In reality this means that it takes about 13 minutes extra to get the same 10-80 charge. Yes that is a decent difference, and I do very much wish the charging was faster - BUT - the only time I use DC chargers is when taking longer journeys and with the Seal that means I need to stop roughly every 3 or so hours for a charge, which is what we do anyway as a family with young kids who need to run around for half an hour to not scream the roof off. So either way, whether we had M3 or Seal our journey routine and length would be pretty much the same. 

- The M3 does have better software without a doubt, no argument from me. But also, I'm buying a car not a phone, the software is only one part of the puzzle and part of the reason the rest of my family said no after the test drive was that the M3 felt too much like a mix between an iPhone and a fridge. It's an appliance made by a tech company, not a car made by an auto-maker. That's not an objectively bad thing, and I personally don't mind it as much being in tech myself - but the rest of my family hated it. And besides, the software in the BYD isn't that bad, hell it's better than most traditional auto-makers and that's more than enough for me. And because it's based on Android I've been able to ADB in and do some interesting stuff. The ADAS in the Tesla is mostly better, but I honestly don't think Tesla Vision is as amazing as a lot of other people do, and it has it's own issues. Most of the Seal's issues come down to calibration, as honestly they've just been lazy on that front and haven't done the hard yards of properly calibrating and programming the ADAS for the different countries environments. In China it works fine, not as good as Tesla still and not as good as some of the other rivals but it's fine which is the only bar I really care about as someone that daily drives another car with 'fine' ADAS systems and doesn't have an issue. 

- The ventilation and heating isn't an issue in Australia, both the long range Premium model (about $3k less than the base M3 here) and the entry level Dynamic model (about $13k less) here come with seat heating and ventilation as standard. 

- As for price see above. I completely understand the calculations being different when pricing is different though, and I would have had a much harder time deciding if I was in the UK or EU. With Australian pricing though it was a no brainer. 

- Rear screen doesn't bother me personally, and I think it looks kind of ugly and tacked on, but it is a cool feature. Netflix and other apps are eventually meant to be coming to the BYD, you can already sideload a bunch of stuff, and there's a browser that you can watch various stuff on built in (I use it mostly for YouTube when charging, but generally I find it easier to just use my phone regardless of Tesla or BYD, ditto for games), Dog mode/camp mode etc are super cool and are a big boon to the Tesla and something I hope comes to the BYD one day, same with Sentry which is an amazing Tesla feature that I genuinely love. No doubt that Tesla offers a lot of cool little functions that are nice to haves. 

- I don't mind one pedal driving, but both my partner and Mum (who will be driving it a lot as we're a multi-generational household) can't stand it on the few cars they've driven with it. Personally I would rather BYD add it and have it able to be turned down, than to just not have it, but it's not a feature I would pay extra for either. I do want to note also that the Seal has just as good regenerative braking as the Model 3, it's just blended into the brake pedal rather than the one pedal system, so you're not losing the actual benefits of regenerative braking, you're just losing using it without using the brake pedal. This was done on purpose to make it feel like a traditional car rather than... well a Tesla - I don't think that's a good or bad thing, it's just a different design choice. 

- Tesla is amazing at efficiency, that absolutely can't be argued. The Seal is pretty good, and is better than most other EV's on that front, but Tesla's are still the kings of efficiency and the amount of range they can pull out of relatively modest batteries is pretty amazing. 

- The difference between the safety scores is hard to compare, Tesla hasn't been tested to NCAP/ANCAP 2023, only 2019 which isn't as strict. The Seal has been, and achieved only a modestly lower rating than what the Model 3 achieved to the less strict 2019 testing. It scored a little worse on adult occupant, the same on child, better on pedestrian, and decently worse on driving assistance - but take that with some salt as that's the area of the testing that has become a lot more strict since 2019. I would say they're pretty equivalent rather than the M3 being outright much better. I would still probably say the Model 3 is slightly safer purely on ADAS, but we'll see how much once it get's retested.

text: @EcoHouseThailand   Yes, but Harry is right here. The reason why needed for me a lot of googeling: The top Voltage of a Lfp Battery is a lot lower than on a Nmc Battery, but the Low end operating Voltage is about the same, so the Range of Voltage between Full and Empty is lower, but the Voltage is with what the Battery Management System is figuring out how much Charge is left and because of the lower range of Voltage it is a lot harder for the Bms with a Lfp Battery to figure out the actuall Charge than with the more often used Nmc Battery. With charging it to 100% the Bms learns best the actual charge and the more often in a row you don't charge to 100% the more little failures are coming in the calculation, which is a lot worse in Lfp Batteries. So because Lfp Batteries lasts 3 times longer than Nmc Batteries, there is no need in protecting the Battery, because the Lfp Battery will easily outlive every car they're in, as Nmc Batterys already nearly do that. So yes, also a Lfp Battery would last longer if you don't charge it to 100%, but it doesn't really matter and you could end up stranded because the Bms calculated the SoC wrong.
